content:
People often ask why we started with excavators. 

Excavators typically make up 20 to 25 percent of the equipment a general contractor operates. They're also one of the hardest machines to learn. An excavator has up to eight axes of motion: the boom, the stick, the bucket, a cab that rotates 360 degrees, and independent tracks. Controlling all of that simultaneously while reading the terrain takes years of practice. Most operators need at least five years to become truly skilled. 

That combination is what makes the excavator the right place to start. It's high volume, high complexity, and high demand. If we can build autonomy that works here, it opens the door to bulldozers, loaders, and every other machine on a job site. 

It's also where the labor gap is especially visible. Skilled heavy equipment operators are some of the hardest roles for contractors to fill, and excavation is critical path on nearly every project. If it falls behind, everything else falls behind with it. 

Excavators are where we start. Autonomous heavy equipment across construction, mining, and beyond is where we're headed.

Morning. We align with the site team (including a superintendent who somehow oversees 10 sites across Texas), walking through scope. We also catch up with Justin Stiehl, who's been a part of our journey from the beginning.

We’ve raised $270 million in Series B funding for Bedrock Robotics to keep building the future of autonomous construction.

This round was co-led by CapitalG, and the Valor Atreides AI Fund (Valor Equity Partners / Atreides Management, LP), with participation from Xora Innovation, 8VC, Eclipse, Emergence Capital, Perry Creek Capital, NVentures (NVIDIA venture capital arm), Tishman Speyer, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Georgian, Incharge Capital Partners, C4 Ventures, and others—bringing our total funding to over $350 million.

Thank you to Michael de la Merced and The New York Times for this morning's thoughtful coverage in Dealbook, linked in the comments below.

The timing here matters. We're entering what may be the largest infrastructure buildout in history—data centers, energy systems, advanced manufacturing, and long-overdue modernization of roads and bridges. The capital and urgency is finally there, but construction needs nearly 800,000 workers over the next two years just to keep pace with today’s demands. 

This funding helps us scale our development and deployments, accelerating toward our first operator-less excavator work on partner sites this year. It's a first step toward a future where fully autonomous fleets could operate as coordinated systems, helping contractors take on more work and changing how they plan, staff, and build.

Thank you to our investors, advisors, and industry partners building alongside us—and to the Bedrock team for enabling this enormous opportunity.

We're not building autonomous equipment. We're building the intelligence layer that could make any equipment autonomous.

article.subtitle: theverge.com
article.linkLabel: Open article: Why the AI era signals the end of the garage founder myth by theverge.com

content:
When I left a prominent role at one of the world’s largest hedge funds to start again in Silicon Valley, I got a lot of funny looks.

When I graduated from Stanford GSB and didn’t go found a software company or PM at Facebook during the heart of the social media boom, and instead took a 24/7 job building factories and advanced manufacturing capabilities at Apple - they laughed at me then too. 

When I doubled down on my hardware / supply chain bet and went to Samsara to build Industrial IOT, creating hardware and generating data for the physical world at the height of the B2B SaaS bonanza, I had people tell me I was actually insane. ‘Throwing away my career! Squandering my opportunity’. (We went public at a $10B valuation 6 years later)

Then - in an ultimate act of folly (?)… I abandoned my hard-won executive leadership position at this winning, soon-to-be public company because … **the opportunity was everywhere, and I couldn’t wait** - single-threading in one company was too slow. 

I wanted to make multiple bets, bring physical-world technologies at every layer of the stack (from silicon to full autonomy and beyond), to every real-world industry. Samsara had proven to me the incredible value to be driven by real-world tech, there was no going back. 

I joined Eclipse - the OG physical world technology investor - because my partners there saw what I saw, and had already been building towards it (investments in blockbuster companies like Cerebras, Wayve , VulcanForms Inc. , Augury)

And now everyone else is realizing what I’ve been called nutso for pursuing over the last 2 decades: That the ultimate value unlock comes from physical-digital convergence. 

It’s time to reinvent the physical world, from healthcare to energy, to manufacturing and transportation… the opportunities are ENDLESS and the TAM is gargantuan. It’s global GDP. 

And we NEED these inventions! Traffic sucks (where my flying car?). Disease is bad (let’s gene edit and manufacture cures). Global supply chains are re-situating (let’s ReIndustrialize). We need to build (how about autonomous excavators! Bedrock Robotics !) 

We’ve been hurtling towards this moment with every technology layer.

And we’re just getting started. 

So, thanks for buying in, @jim kramer! I guess my mission is finally mainstream now :-)

The extension: https://lnkd.in/epwZh8aN

Use it to:
- Look up companies and their funding history
- Look up other investors and figure out what they’re actually doing
- Build the right list of investors for your companies when they’re ready to raise

The Codex is free for now. So is the extension we built for it. It could definitely be better. Tell us how.

P.S. about the data:
- If you spot any incorrect data, tell us and we’ll fix it.
- The Codex relies on publicly announced rounds, so if a round isn't disclosed or some investors aren't listed, the data may be incomplete.
- Investor titles and affiliations change frequently. We update these through sweeps of VC websites, but it takes time to capture every change.
